Does the Analysis Recover a Known Effect?

Source: R/evidence.R
cpsplant.Rd

Plants effects of known size into the real data and checks that the statistic gets them back. Each planted data set keeps every column as it is, except the outcome: it is shuffled, which removes whatever real association it had with the treatment, and then the planted effect is added, effect * treatment. A statistic that estimates the treatment's effect on the outcome should return about effect on every one.

Usage

cpsplant(
  data,
  stat,
  y,
  trt,
  effects = c(0, 0.5, 1),
  n = 50L,
  tol = NULL,
  seed = NULL
)

Arguments

data

A data frame with at least 4 rows.

stat

A function of one data frame returning one number: the estimated effect of trt on y.

y

The outcome column's name. It must be numeric.

trt

The treatment column's name.

effects

The effects to plant. Include 0, so a statistic that finds an effect where there is none fails.

n

Planted data sets per effect.

tol

How far an average estimate may sit from the planted effect. The default is 10% of the largest planted effect.

seed

Optional seed, for a reproducible check. The session's own random stream is left as it was.

Value

A list of class rmbl_plant: ok (every effect recovered), table (one row per effect: effect, recovered (the average estimate), bias, se, passed), observed (the statistic on the real data), n, tol, y, trt and seed. It prints as a box and goes into a manifest with recevid().

Details

This is evidence about the statistic as it is applied to this data (its missing values, its skew, its group sizes), which a simulation on made-up data cannot give. A statistic that recovers 0, 0.5 and 1 correctly is very unlikely to be computing the wrong thing.

The treatment column must be numeric, logical or a factor with two levels (the second is coded 1). Effects are on the outcome's own scale per unit of treatment, so the statistic must estimate an additive effect: a difference in means, a regression slope, an average treatment effect. An estimate passes when it is within tol of the planted effect, after allowing three Monte Carlo standard errors.

See also

cpsspec() for agreement across specifications, cpsfals() for falsification controls, recevid() to record them all.

Examples

set.seed(1)
d <- data.frame(x = rbinom(200, 1, 0.5), z = rnorm(200))
d$y <- 2 * d$x + d$z + rnorm(200)

# A difference in means recovers what is planted.
dm <- function(df) mean(df$y[df$x == 1]) - mean(df$y[df$x == 0])
cpsplant(d, dm, y = "y", trt = "x", n = 30, seed = 1)
#> ╭── Planted-effect recovery: passed ──────────────────────────────────────────╮
#> │ ✔ VERIFIED                                                                  │
#> │                                                                             │
#> │   Outcome                    y                                              │
#> │   Treatment                  x                                              │
#> │   Data sets per effect       30                                             │
#> │   Tolerance                  0.1                                            │
#> │   Estimate on the real data  1.754                                          │
#> │   Seed                       1                                              │
#> │                                                                             │
#> │   planted  recovered      bias       se  result                             │
#> │   -------  ---------  --------  -------  ------                             │
#> │    0.0000     0.0565   0.05647  0.04314  ok                                 │
#> │    0.5000     0.4977  -0.00234  0.04137  ok                                 │
#> │    1.0000     1.0616   0.06160  0.04818  ok                                 │
#> │                                                                             │
#> │   The statistic recovered every planted effect on this data, so it          │
#> │   measures the treatment's effect on the outcome as intended.               │
#> │                                                                             │
#> │   Each planted data set shuffles the outcome, removing its real             │
#> │   association, then adds effect x treatment.                                │
#> ╰─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯

# A statistic with a bug (it doubles the effect) does not.
bad <- function(df) 2 * dm(df)
cpsplant(d, bad, y = "y", trt = "x", n = 30, seed = 1)$ok
#> [1] FALSE
